claim: Exposure to stress increases the risk of developing mood disorders.
source: Exposure to stress increases the risk of developing mood disorders.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the relationship between stress and mood disorders.

claim: A subset of individuals displays vulnerability to stress while others remain resilient.
source: While a subset of individuals displays vulnerability to stress, others remain resilient, but the molecular basis for these behavioral differences is not well understood.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of stress research.

claim: The molecular basis for behavioral differences between stress-vulnerable and stress-resilient individuals is not well understood.
source: While a subset of individuals displays vulnerability to stress, others remain resilient, but the molecular basis for these behavioral differences is not well understood.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of scientific knowledge and identifies a gap in understanding.

claim: Region-specific differences in myelination exist between susceptible and resilient mice following chronic social defeat stress.
source: Using a model of chronic social defeat stress, we identified region-specific differences in myelination between mice that displayed social avoidance behavior ('susceptible') and those who escaped the deleterious effect to stress ('resilient').
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Myelin protein content in the nucleus accumbens was reduced in all mice exposed to stress.
source: Myelin protein content in the nucleus accumbens was reduced in all mice exposed to stress, whereas decreased myelin thickness and internodal length were detected only in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) of susceptible mice, with fewer mature oligodendrocytes and decreased heterochromatic histone marks.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Decreased myelin thickness and internodal length were detected only in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) of susceptible mice.
source: Myelin protein content in the nucleus accumbens was reduced in all mice exposed to stress, whereas decreased myelin thickness and internodal length were detected only in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) of susceptible mice, with fewer mature oligodendrocytes and decreased heterochromatic histone marks.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Susceptible mice have fewer mature oligodendrocytes in the mPFC.
source: Myelin protein content in the nucleus accumbens was reduced in all mice exposed to stress, whereas decreased myelin thickness and internodal length were detected only in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) of susceptible mice, with fewer mature oligodendrocytes and decreased heterochromatic histone marks.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Susceptible mice have decreased heterochromatic histone marks in the mPFC.
source: Myelin protein content in the nucleus accumbens was reduced in all mice exposed to stress, whereas decreased myelin thickness and internodal length were detected only in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) of susceptible mice, with fewer mature oligodendrocytes and decreased heterochromatic histone marks.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: Focal demyelination in the mPFC is sufficient to decrease social preference.
source: Focal demyelination in the mPFC was sufficient to decrease social preference, which was restored following new myelin formation.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Social preference is restored following new myelin formation in the mPFC.
source: Focal demyelination in the mPFC was sufficient to decrease social preference, which was restored following new myelin formation.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: mPFC myelination is a critical determinant of the avoidance response to traumatic social experiences.
source: Together these data highlight the functional role of mPFC myelination as critical determinant of the avoidance response to traumatic social experiences.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study, particularly the demyelination experiments.

claim: Differences in behavioral response to stress can be detected in experimental mouse models.
source: Differences in the behavioral response to stress can also be detected in experimental mouse models, thereby highlighting the degree of conservation of this response.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of stress research using animal models.

claim: The behavioral response to stress is conserved between humans and mice.
source: Differences in the behavioral response to stress can also be detected in experimental mouse models, thereby highlighting the degree of conservation of this response.
evidence: This is inferred from the statement about conservation of stress responses across species.

claim: Animal models of psychosocial stressors lead to transcriptional, translational, or ultrastructural changes in oligodendrocytes and myelination.
source: We and others have previously reported that animal models of psychosocial stressors, such as social isolation (Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2016; Makinodan et al., 2016; Makinodan et al., 2017; Makinodan et al., 2012), chronic social defeat stress (CSDS) (Cathomas et al., 2019; Lehmann et al., 2017), and chronic variable stress (Liu et al., 2018), lead to transcriptional, translational, or ultrastructural changes in oligodendrocytes and myelination.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Social isolation leads to changes in oligodendrocytes and myelination.
source: We and others have previously reported that animal models of psychosocial stressors, such as social isolation (Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2016; Makinodan et al., 2016; Makinodan et al., 2017; Makinodan et al., 2012), chronic social defeat stress (CSDS) (Cathomas et al., 2019; Lehmann et al., 2017), and chronic variable stress (Liu et al., 2018), lead to transcriptional, translational, or ultrastructural changes in oligodendrocytes and myelination.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Chronic social defeat stress (CSDS) leads to changes in oligodendrocytes and myelination.
source: We and others have previously reported that animal models of psychosocial stressors, such as social isolation (Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2016; Makinodan et al., 2016; Makinodan et al., 2017; Makinodan et al., 2012), chronic social defeat stress (CSDS) (Cathomas et al., 2019; Lehmann et al., 2017), and chronic variable stress (Liu et al., 2018), lead to transcriptional, translational, or ultrastructural changes in oligodendrocytes and myelination.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Chronic variable stress leads to changes in oligodendrocytes and myelination.
source: We and others have previously reported that animal models of psychosocial stressors, such as social isolation (Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2016; Makinodan et al., 2016; Makinodan et al., 2017; Makinodan et al., 2012), chronic social defeat stress (CSDS) (Cathomas et al., 2019; Lehmann et al., 2017), and chronic variable stress (Liu et al., 2018), lead to transcriptional, translational, or ultrastructural changes in oligodendrocytes and myelination.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The nucleus accumbens and medial prefrontal cortex play a critical role in determining stress responses.
source: We focused our analysis on the nucleus accumbens (NAc) and the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), two brain regions shown to play a critical role in determining stress responses (Heshmati et al., 2018; Han and Nestler, 2017) and displaying myelin transcriptional or structural impairment after a stressful experience (Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2016; Makinodan et al., 2016; Lehmann et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The nucleus accumbens and medial prefrontal cortex display myelin transcriptional or structural impairment after a stressful experience.
source: We focused our analysis on the nucleus accumbens (NAc) and the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), two brain regions shown to play a critical role in determining stress responses (Heshmati et al., 2018; Han and Nestler, 2017) and displaying myelin transcriptional or structural impairment after a stressful experience (Liu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2016; Makinodan et al., 2016; Lehmann et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mice were exposed to an aggressor challenge for 10 days in the chronic social defeat stress model.
source: We adopted a mouse model of chronic social defeat stress (CSDS) (Golden et al., 2011), in which mice were exposed to an aggressor challenge for 10 days (Figure 1A) and tested for social behavior afterwards.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used in the study, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Some mice showed signs of social withdrawal characterized by reduced social interaction time and reduced social interaction ratio (susceptible mice).
source: While some mice showed signs of social withdrawal, characterized by reduced social interaction time when a conspecific mouse is present and reduced social interaction ratio (i.e. susceptible mice), a subset escaped this deleterious consequence (i.e. resilient mice), and were virtually indistinguishable from the control group, which were not exposed to any aggressors (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Resilient mice were virtually indistinguishable from the control group in social behavior.
source: While some mice showed signs of social withdrawal, characterized by reduced social interaction time when a conspecific mouse is present and reduced social interaction ratio (i.e. susceptible mice), a subset escaped this deleterious consequence (i.e. resilient mice), and were virtually indistinguishable from the control group, which were not exposed to any aggressors (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Susceptible mice spent less time interacting with a conspecific mouse than control or resilient mice (p<0.0001).
source: Control, n = 52; susceptible, n = 39; resilient, n = 33; ****, p<0.0001 by one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post hoc test.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: MBP levels in the NAc were significantly reduced in susceptible mice compared to controls (p=0.0447).
source: n = 3 mice per group, two 20x images per animal; susceptible vs. control, p=0.0447; resilient vs. control, p=0.0109 by one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post hoc test.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: MBP levels in the NAc were significantly reduced in resilient mice compared to controls (p=0.0109).
source: n = 3 mice per group, two 20x images per animal; susceptible vs. control, p=0.0447; resilient vs. control, p=0.0109 by one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post hoc test.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: No significant differences were detected in the length of myelinated segments in the NAc among groups.
source: However, no significant differences were detected in the length of myelinated segments measured by MBP immunoreactivity (Figure 1F–H) or in myelin thickness (Figure 1I–K) among groups.
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in Figure 1F-H.

claim: No significant differences were detected in myelin thickness in the NAc among groups.
source: However, no significant differences were detected in the length of myelinated segments measured by MBP immunoreactivity (Figure 1F–H) or in myelin thickness (Figure 1I–K) among groups.
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in Figure 1I-K.

claim: There is no significant correlation between the length of MBP-covered segments and social interaction ratio in control mice (r = −0.2242, p=0.5934).
source: Pearson coefficients correlation showed no significant correlation between the length of MBP-covered segments and social interaction ratio in either control or defeated group (control, r = −0.2242, p=0.5934, defeated, r = −0.3483, p-0.3240, Figure 1G–H).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis result from the experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: There is no significant correlation between the length of MBP-covered segments and social interaction ratio in defeated mice (r = −0.3483, p=0.3240).
source: Pearson coefficients correlation showed no significant correlation between the length of MBP-covered segments and social interaction ratio in either control or defeated group (control, r = −0.2242, p=0.5934, defeated, r = −0.3483, p-0.3240, Figure 1G–H).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis result from the experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Myelination in the NAc uniformly responds to stress and does not distinguish susceptibility and resilience following CSDS.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that myelination in the NAc uniformly responds to stress and does not distinguish susceptibility and resilience following CSDS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on NAc myelination.

claim: The mPFC displayed a unique myelination phenotype following CSDS.
source: In contrast, the mPFC displayed a unique myelination phenotype following CSDS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing mPFC data to NAc data.

claim: MBP levels in the mPFC did not significantly differ between susceptible and resilient mice.
source: While the levels of MBP did not significantly differ between susceptible and resilient mice (control, 6.2 ± 0.5%; susceptible, 6.1 ± 0.9%; resilient, 5.3 ± 0.8%; Figure 2A–B), the length of myelinated segments indicated by MBP immunoreactivity showed a significant positive correlation with social interaction in defeated mice (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: The length of myelinated segments in the mPFC showed a significant positive correlation with social interaction in defeated mice.
source: While the levels of MBP did not significantly differ between susceptible and resilient mice (control, 6.2 ± 0.5%; susceptible, 6.1 ± 0.9%; resilient, 5.3 ± 0.8%; Figure 2A–B), the length of myelinated segments indicated by MBP immunoreactivity showed a significant positive correlation with social interaction in defeated mice (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis result from the experimental data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: No correlation between myelinated segment length and social interaction was detected in the control (unstressed) group in the mPFC.
source: Importantly, such correlation was not detected in the control (unstressed) group, suggesting that changes in the length of myelinated segments represent an adaptive response to the social defeat stress.
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Changes in the length of myelinated segments in the mPFC represent an adaptive response to social defeat stress.
source: Importantly, such correlation was not detected in the control (unstressed) group, suggesting that changes in the length of myelinated segments represent an adaptive response to the social defeat stress.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data based on the differential correlation patterns.

claim: A significant positive correlation between internodal length and social interaction ratio was detected only in defeated mice in the mPFC.
source: Also in this case, a significant positive correlation between internodal length and social interaction ratio was detected only in the defeated mice, with shorter internodal lengths identified in susceptible mice (Figure 2G–H).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis result from the experimental data shown in Figure 2G-H.

claim: Shorter internodal lengths were identified in susceptible mice in the mPFC.
source: Also in this case, a significant positive correlation between internodal length and social interaction ratio was detected only in the defeated mice, with shorter internodal lengths identified in susceptible mice (Figure 2G–H).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in Figure 2G-H.

claim: Myelin was thinner in susceptible mice compared to controls in the mPFC (p=0.0264).
source: Myelin was also thinner in the susceptible - but not in the resilient – mice, compared to controls (Figure 2I–K).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data shown in Figure 2I-K.

claim: Myelin was not thinner in resilient mice compared to controls in the mPFC.
source: Myelin was also thinner in the susceptible - but not in the resilient – mice, compared to controls (Figure 2I–K).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in Figure 2I-K.

claim: Region-specific myelination differences in the mPFC could at least in part explain the behavioral differences between susceptible and resilient mice in response to stress.
source: Therefore, region-specific myelination differences in the mPFC could -at least in part- explain the behavioral differences between susceptible and resilient mice in response to stress.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on mPFC myelination and behavior.

claim: No significant difference in the overall number of OLIG2+ cells was detected in the mPFC among groups.
source: No significant difference in the overall number of OLIG2+ cells was detected (Figure 3A,C), thereby ruling out decreased survival of oligodendrocyte lineage cells in response to stress.
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in Figure 3A,C.

claim: Decreased survival of oligodendrocyte lineage cells in response to stress is ruled out.
source: No significant difference in the overall number of OLIG2+ cells was detected (Figure 3A,C), thereby ruling out decreased survival of oligodendrocyte lineage cells in response to stress.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the OLIG2+ cell count data.

claim: Susceptible mice had a significantly higher number of NG2+ progenitor cells in the mPFC compared to resilient and control mice.
source: However, compared to resilient and controls, the susceptible mice were characterized by a significantly higher number of NG2+ progenitor cells (control, 39.2 ± 2.3 mm−2; susceptible, 55.3 ± 4.4 mm−2; resilient, 25.8 ± 4.8 mm−2; Figure 3A,C), and lower number of CC1+ mature oligodendrocytes (control, 91.9 ± 5.7 mm−2; susceptible, 62.7 ± 5.2 mm−2; resilient, 86.1 ± 5.8 mm−2; Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in Figure 3A,C.

claim: Susceptible mice had a lower number of CC1+ mature oligodendrocytes in the mPFC compared to resilient and control mice.
source: However, compared to resilient and controls, the susceptible mice were characterized by a significantly higher number of NG2+ progenitor cells (control, 39.2 ± 2.3 mm−2; susceptible, 55.3 ± 4.4 mm−2; resilient, 25.8 ± 4.8 mm−2; Figure 3A,C), and lower number of CC1+ mature oligodendrocytes (control, 91.9 ± 5.7 mm−2; susceptible, 62.7 ± 5.2 mm−2; resilient, 86.1 ± 5.8 mm−2; Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: A reduction of H3K9me3 histone modification marks was detected in the mPFC of susceptible mice.
source: Consistent with defective differentiation of NG2+ cells in the mPFC of susceptible mice, a reduction of the histone modification marks associated with differentiation (H3K9me3) was also detected (pixel/area: control, 1373.6 ± 113.3; susceptible, 695.3 ± 127.9; resilient, 1186.0 ± 106.0; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Social stress promotes myelin remodeling resulting in shorter internodal length and fewer wraps in the mPFC.
source: Together these data suggest that social stress might have at least two main effects on oligodendrocyte lineage cells in the mPFC: it promotes myelin remodeling resulting in shorter internodal length and fewer wraps and possibly impairs in the epigenetic program of oligodendrocyte progenitor differentiation, resulting in fewer differentiated oligodendrocytes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on myelin structure.

claim: Social stress possibly impairs the epigenetic program of oligodendrocyte progenitor differentiation in the mPFC, resulting in fewer differentiated oligodendrocytes.
source: Together these data suggest that social stress might have at least two main effects on oligodendrocyte lineage cells in the mPFC: it promotes myelin remodeling resulting in shorter internodal length and fewer wraps and possibly impairs in the epigenetic program of oligodendrocyte progenitor differentiation, resulting in fewer differentiated oligodendrocytes.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the experimental data on oligodendrocyte populations and epigenetic marks.

claim: LPC injection is a well characterized model of toxic demyelination.
source: LPC injection is a well characterized model of toxic demyelination, with early myelin loss (detectable one week after injection) followed by spontaneous repair, due to the formation of new myelin by newly differentiated oligodendrocytes (occurring three weeks after injection) (Jeffery and Blakemore, 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: LPC injection causes early myelin loss detectable one week after injection.
source: LPC injection is a well characterized model of toxic demyelination, with early myelin loss (detectable one week after injection) followed by spontaneous repair, due to the formation of new myelin by newly differentiated oligodendrocytes (occurring three weeks after injection) (Jeffery and Blakemore, 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: LPC injection is followed by spontaneous repair occurring three weeks after injection.
source: LPC injection is a well characterized model of toxic demyelination, with early myelin loss (detectable one week after injection) followed by spontaneous repair, due to the formation of new myelin by newly differentiated oligodendrocytes (occurring three weeks after injection) (Jeffery and Blakemore, 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: Spontaneous repair after LPC injection is due to the formation of new myelin by newly differentiated oligodendrocytes.
source: LPC injection is a well characterized model of toxic demyelination, with early myelin loss (detectable one week after injection) followed by spontaneous repair, due to the formation of new myelin by newly differentiated oligodendrocytes (occurring three weeks after injection) (Jeffery and Blakemore, 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: The kinetics of demyelination and remyelination after LPC injection was validated by reduced MBP immunoreactivity at 7dpi followed by spontaneous recovery by 21dpi.
source: Indeed, the kinetics of demyelination and remyelination after LPC injection was validated by the detection of reduced MBP immunoreactivity at the 7dpi followed by spontaneous recovery of immunoreactivity by 21dpi (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: LPC-injected mice displayed reduced social preference behavior at 7dpi compared to saline-injected controls.
source: At the early time point (7dpi), LPC-injected mice displayed reduced social preference behavior compared to saline-injected controls (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The difference in social interaction behavior between LPC-injected and saline-injected mice was no longer detectable after 3 weeks.
source: This difference in social interaction behavior was no longer detectable after 3 weeks (Figure 4D), when myelination recovered to normal level (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Myelination recovered to normal level by 21dpi after LPC injection.
source: This difference in social interaction behavior was no longer detectable after 3 weeks (Figure 4D), when myelination recovered to normal level (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Myelin content in the mPFC is a critical determinant of social behavior.
source: Therefore, we conclude that myelin content in the mPFC is a critical determinant of social behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the LPC injection experiments showing causal relationship.

claim: Myelination defects were detected in socially isolated adult mice prior to the appearance of social avoidance behavior.
source: We have previously reported that myelination defects were detected in socially isolated adult mice, prior to the appearance of social avoidance behavior (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a reference to previous research by the authors.

claim: Social avoidance behavior can be detected after chronic social defeat stress.
source: Here, we show that social avoidance behavior can be detected after chronic social defeat stress as well as after focal demyelination in the mPFC, and could therefore be caused by hypomyelination.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in the current study.

claim: Social avoidance behavior can be detected after focal demyelination in the mPFC.
source: Here, we show that social avoidance behavior can be detected after chronic social defeat stress as well as after focal demyelination in the mPFC, and could therefore be caused by hypomyelination.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in the current study.

claim: Social avoidance behavior could be caused by hypomyelination.
source: Here, we show that social avoidance behavior can be detected after chronic social defeat stress as well as after focal demyelination in the mPFC, and could therefore be caused by hypomyelination.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing correlation and causation.

claim: Promoting myelination has been shown to rescue depressive-like behavior in socially isolated mice.
source: Furthermore, promoting myelination has been shown to rescue depressive-like behavior in socially isolated mice (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a reference to previous research by the authors.

claim: Normal social behavior was restored following spontaneously occurring remyelination in LPC-injected mice.
source: On the same note, normal social behavior was restored following the spontaneously occurring remyelination in LPC-injected mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: Social stress did not induce a toxic effect on myelin.
source: However, it is important to note that, social stress did not induce a toxic effect on myelin, whereas LPC did.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the effects of social stress and LPC on myelin.

claim: LPC induced a toxic effect on myelin.
source: However, it is important to note that, social stress did not induce a toxic effect on myelin, whereas LPC did.
evidence: This is established knowledge about LPC effects and confirmed by the experimental data.

claim: No cellular toxicity was detected in the mPFC of susceptible mice.
source: No cellular toxicity was detected in the mPFC of susceptible mice or in mice undergoing social isolation (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the current study and previous research.

claim: No cellular toxicity was detected in mice undergoing social isolation.
source: No cellular toxicity was detected in the mPFC of susceptible mice or in mice undergoing social isolation (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a reference to previous research by the authors.

claim: The lower myelin content in the mPFC of susceptible mice results from impaired oligodendrocyte progenitor differentiation.
source: For this reason, we interpret the lower myelin content in the mPFC of susceptible mice as resulting from impaired oligodendrocyte progenitor differentiation, possibly as maladaptive response to social stress.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data on oligodendrocyte populations and epigenetic marks.

claim: Impaired oligodendrocyte progenitor differentiation in susceptible mice is possibly a maladaptive response to social stress.
source: For this reason, we interpret the lower myelin content in the mPFC of susceptible mice as resulting from impaired oligodendrocyte progenitor differentiation, possibly as maladaptive response to social stress.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Reorganization of paranodal loops could be affected in susceptible mice.
source: While our data support an inefficient production of new myelin, the detection of a positive correlation between intermodal length and social avoidance behavior, suggests that reorganization of paranodal loops could also be affected.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the correlation data.

claim: Shorter internodal length consequent to impaired myelin formation has been shown to decrease nerve conduction in the optic nerve.
source: Indeed, shorter internodal length, consequent to impaired myelin formation, has been previously shown to decrease nerve conduction in the optic nerve (Etxeberria et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a reference to previous research.

claim: The reduced length of myelinated segments detected in the mPFC of susceptible mice may result in slower conduction.
source: It is, therefore, conceivable that the reduced length of myelinated segments detected in the mPFC of susceptible mice may result in slower conduction and functionally result in the characteristic social avoidance behavior in response to the social stress.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental data and previous research on conduction velocity.

claim: Reduced length of myelinated segments in the mPFC of susceptible mice may functionally result in social avoidance behavior.
source: It is, therefore, conceivable that the reduced length of myelinated segments detected in the mPFC of susceptible mice may result in slower conduction and functionally result in the characteristic social avoidance behavior in response to the social stress.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental data and previous research.

claim: New myelin is formed in the mPFC of resilient mice as an adaptive mechanism to repeated episodes of aggression.
source: Finally, we suggest that new myelin is formed in the mPFC of resilient mice as an adaptive mechanism to the repeated episodes of aggression.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental data on resilient mice.

claim: The formation of new myelin in resilient mice could favor the establishment of neuronal circuits allowing escape from negative impact following traumatic stress.
source: It is conceivable that the formation of new myelin in resilient mice could favor the establishment of neuronal circuits allowing the escape of negative impact following traumatic stress (Krishnan et al., 2007; Fagundes et al., 2013; Fenster et al., 2018; Ménard et al., 2017; Russo et al., 2012), as oligodendrocytes are known to regulate conduction speed and play a crucial role in synchronizing neuronal networks (Saab and Nave, 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Oligodendrocytes are known to regulate conduction speed and play a crucial role in synchronizing neuronal networks.
source: It is conceivable that the formation of new myelin in resilient mice could favor the establishment of neuronal circuits allowing the escape of negative impact following traumatic stress (Krishnan et al., 2007; Fagundes et al., 2013; Fenster et al., 2018; Ménard et al., 2017; Russo et al., 2012), as oligodendrocytes are known to regulate conduction speed and play a crucial role in synchronizing neuronal networks (Saab and Nave, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: Stress resilience may arise from active coping strategies rather than a passive response.
source: This explanation is in agreement with the increasing evidence from mice and squirrel monkeys, which suggests stress resilience may arise from active coping strategies, rather than a passive response, defined as lack of adaptive response (Russo et al., 2012; Lyons et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The molecular basis for resilience has been studied extensively in the context of neuronal cells, the immune and neuroendocrine systems.
source: The molecular basis for resilience has been studied extensively in the context of neuronal cells, the immune and neuroendocrine systems (Ménard et al., 2017; Russo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: New myelin formation as a coping strategy may be associated with increased neuronal activity in resilient mice.
source: One possibility for new myelin formation as a coping strategy is associated with increased neuronal activity in the resilient mice, as reported by a greater degree of FosB, or ΔFosB expression in glutamatergic neurons of mPFC of resilient mice following social defeat (Covington et al., 2010; Lehmann and Herkenham, 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Resilient mice show a greater degree of FosB or ΔFosB expression in glutamatergic neurons of mPFC following social defeat.
source: One possibility for new myelin formation as a coping strategy is associated with increased neuronal activity in the resilient mice, as reported by a greater degree of FosB, or ΔFosB expression in glutamatergic neurons of mPFC of resilient mice following social defeat (Covington et al., 2010; Lehmann and Herkenham, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of mPFC has been shown to help resilience phenotype in social defeated mice.
source: Optogenetic stimulation of mPFC has been shown to help resilience phenotype in social defeated mice (Covington et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation has been shown to promote oligodendrogliogenesis and new myelin formation.
source: Although not characterized in the previous study (Covington et al., 2010), optogenetic stimulation has been shown to promote oligodendrogliogenesis and new myelin formation (Gibson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: IL-6 has been identified as a major cytokine that contributes to the development of depression in humans.
source: An alternative mechanism could involve inflammatory cytokines, such as interleukin-6 (IL-6). IL-6 has been identified as a major cytokine that contributes to the development of depression in human (Dowlati et al., 2010; Erta et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Systemic IL-6 was the only differentially regulated cytokine that distinguished resilient mice from susceptible and control mice in animal models of stress.
source: In animal models of stress, systemic IL-6, was the only differentially regulated cytokine that distinguished resilient mice from susceptible and control mice (Hodes et al., 2014).
